power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Mean Length Utterance (MLU) is a common measure of syntactic complexity in studies of children's language development.
It is often used by the clinical community, including speech-language pathologists in the diagnosis of children's speech disorders (e.g., Rice et al. 2006; Hernandez et al., 2024).
text.formatted: It is often used by the clinical community, including speech-language pathologists in the diagnosis of children's speech disorders (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Rice et al. 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hernandez et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In its original formulation, Brown (1973) proposed MLU as the typical number of morphemes of English per utterance in a child's speech as a means of measuring emerging syntactic complexity.
text.formatted: In its original formulation, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown (1973)</ref> proposed MLU as the typical number of morphemes of English per utterance in a child's speech as a means of measuring emerging syntactic complexity.

text.text: His original proposal was to calculate the MLU for a speaker by counting the total number of morphemes in the speech sample and dividing by the number of utterances.
The underlying logic is the implication that the number of units occurring together is directly proportional to grammatical complexity.
While Brown himself did not specify what constituted an utterance, Miller (1981) proposed that utterance boundaries may be based on intonations and pauses between utterances.
text.formatted: While Brown himself did not specify what constituted an utterance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Miller (1981)</ref> proposed that utterance boundaries may be based on intonations and pauses between utterances.

text.text: Since this original measure was proposed, MLU has been computed in myriad ways, with different authors using different operationalisations of the measure (e.g., MLU of longest 3 utterances; subsampling from the first 50 utterances; see more below).

While all operationalisations aim to capture something about grammatical complexity in early development, each metric reflects different underlying assumptions about properties of the data distribution, and the intended targets of the metric.

Furthermore, while this measure has been useful in characterising the grammatical complexity of English-speaking children (e.g., Guo & Eisenberg, 2015; Miller & Chapman, 1981), it is difficult to implement in language communities whose language features do not map on to that of English.
text.formatted: Furthermore, while this measure has been useful in characterising the grammatical complexity of English-speaking children (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Guo & Eisenberg, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Miller & Chapman, 1981)</ref>, it is difficult to implement in language communities whose language features do not map on to that of English.

text.text: This challenge is further compounded when we consider multilingual communities who make use of all their languages variably within and across utterances.
There are three aims of this paper.
First, we provide some current examples of how MLU is defined, used and collected in the field of child language development.

We then explore measurement characteristics of MLU-like metrics in a large corpus of child-directed speech from parents in multilingual Singapore and explain the challenges of implementing commonly used MLU metrics to our multilingual translanguaging-heavy dataset.

Next, using our dataset as an example, we show that these MLU-like metrics are better suited as measures of grammatical complexity and offer suggestions for researchers and clinicians who are looking for new ways to examine grammatical complexity and/or also work in bi/multilingual communities.

Finally, to help researchers and clinicians make principled decisions, we simulate a few conditions for selecting the most appropriate MLU-like metrics depending on key factors: the specific linguistic metrics of interest, characteristics of the study population, and practical considerations such as time and manpower.

Based on the results of these simulations, we present a decision tree as a reproducible, pre-registerable pathway to aid researchers in selecting the most suitable MLU-like syntactic complexity metric across diverse language data types, including varying sample sizes, transcription depth, and linguistic contexts.

In the section that follows, we provide a brief non-exhaustive review of some current definitions and operationalisations of measures of complexity, with a count of the papers that use each type, graphically summarised in Figure 1.

text.text: In designing an MLU study or in clinical applications using MLUlike metrics, the kinds of sample and the context of the sample can vary widely.

The method of speech elicitation for children or adult-child dyads includes naturalistic speech with a caregiver such as free play sessions (e.g., Rollins et al., 1996), picture naming tasks (e.g., Goh et al., 2008), wordlesspicture-book sharing (e.g., Woon et al., 2021), and more targeted interactions in a clinical setting with a speech-language pathologist (e.g., Sanz-Torrent et al., 2008).
text.formatted: The method of speech elicitation for children or adult-child dyads includes naturalistic speech with a caregiver such as free play sessions (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rollins et al., 1996)</ref>, picture naming tasks (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Goh et al., 2008)</ref>, wordlesspicture-book sharing (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Woon et al., 2021)</ref>, and more targeted interactions in a clinical setting with a speech-language pathologist (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Sanz-Torrent et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These different elicitation strategies may have different implications for the time available for speech sampling, as well as for the child's level of comfort during the task.

In our review of the existing literature, we observed seven different approaches of types of speech elicitation activities and three combinations of speech-target (whose speech is being analysed) and interlocutors (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: In our review of the existing literature, we observed seven different approaches of types of speech elicitation activities and three combinations of speech-target (whose speech is being analysed) and interlocutors (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Each of these approaches and speech-targets results in different amounts of data available for analysis and different resulting counts.

We expect that in multilingual communities, there is a greater challenge in selecting suitable speech elicitation tasks or speech-targets for analysis as children and caregivers may not feel comfortable using their "home" language (e.g., native languages, informal varieties, or translanguaged speech) in front of unfamiliar adults or clinicians.
One way of overcoming this observer bias is to conduct daylong recordings with small speech recorders.

Over the course of the day, participants (typically children) wearing the recorders and their interlocutors forget or pay no attention to the presence of the recorders which then lead to recordings which better reflect language use at home by the child and their caregivers (e.g., Casillas, 2023; Cychosz et al., 2021).

text.text: Approach to measurement.

Since the origins of the MLU metric, researchers have taken different approaches regarding the participants who would be the target of the research, as well as the measurement unit (e.g., morphemes) and span (e.g., utterances) over which the measure of syntactic complexity was computed.

While the majority of studies on grammatical complexity investigate the MLU of children at different stages of development (e.g., de Villiers & de Villiers, 1973; Heilmann et al., 2010), some studies have used MLU to investigate the grammatical complexity of parental speech in child-directed speech (Baker et al., 2015; Bingham et al., 2012; Hoff, 2003; Hoff & Naigles, 2002; Taumoepeau, 2006; Taylor et al., 2009).

text.text: In terms of measuring the unit of speech, strategies include morphemes (e.g., Brown, 1973), words (e.g., Wu, 2020) or counting syllables (e.g., Cheung, 1998), and these strategies were likely chosen to suit different languages or different research contexts.
text.formatted: In terms of measuring the unit of speech, strategies include morphemes (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown, 1973)</ref>, words (e.g., Wu, 2020) or counting syllables (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Cheung, 1998)</ref>, and these strategies were likely chosen to suit different languages or different research contexts.

text.text: For example, when working with written transcripts, word counts are transparent in transcripts of English, as word boundaries are marked by spaces, while syllable and morpheme counts are more difficult to derive, as morpheme boundaries are not always clear.
Hence, a researcher working with written English transcripts may choose to use word counts instead of morpheme counts as their measure of language use or language complexity.

On the other hand, syllable counts are transparent in transcripts of Chinese, as each syllable of Chinese is represented by a single written character, while word and morpheme counts are more difficult to derive, as word boundaries are not marked.
So, researchers working with Chinese scripts may prefer using syllable counts.

For teams working with audio recordings instead of written transcripts, some automated data pipelines have been used to estimate the number of syllables in a span of speech from the raw audio (e.g., de Jong & Wempe, 2009).
text.formatted: For teams working with audio recordings instead of written transcripts, some automated data pipelines have been used to estimate the number of syllables in a span of speech from the raw audio (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">de Jong & Wempe, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: However, due to differences in language structures, and the baseline data on which an automated pipeline was trained, these pipelines are not a one-size-fits-all solution and manual processing of audio recordings remains necessary.

Regardless of language, the measurement of units of speech is further complicated when different automated models disagree on the number of words or morphemes in a particular token, or in a particular variety (see Choo et al., forthcoming for details).
text.formatted: Regardless of language, the measurement of units of speech is further complicated when different automated models disagree on the number of words or morphemes in a particular token, or in a particular variety (see <ref type="bibr">Choo et al.</ref>, forthcoming for details).

text.text: In terms of the span of connected speech over which the units are sampled, some researchers have focused on utterances, which are defined pragmatically (e.g., Miller 1981), while others have focused on sentences or clauses, which are defined syntactically (e.g., Guo & Eisenberg, 2015).
text.formatted: In terms of the span of connected speech over which the units are sampled, some researchers have focused on utterances, which are defined pragmatically (e.g., Miller 1981), while others have focused on sentences or clauses, which are defined syntactically (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Guo & Eisenberg, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Syntactic units such as 'clause' and 'sentence' may be more straightforward to determine in linguistic varieties with well documented subject-prominent grammars such as Standard English (e.g., Li & Thompson, 1976), whereas this metric may be less straightforward in languages which feature topic-comment grammar such as Mandarin Chinese (e.g., Shi, 2000), and informal Singapore English (e.g., Chang, 2009; see also Ng, 2024 for a discussion of topic-comment sentence constructions in parent-child talk in Singapore).

text.text: In addition to the challenge of parsing different units and spans from transcripts of different languages, it should be noted that typologically distinct languages have different measurement properties across the different metrics.

For example, when comparing MLU-words-per-utterance to MLU-morphemes-per-utterance, a highly agglutinatingfoot_0 language such as Tamil would have a much larger difference between the two metrics, while a more isolating language such as English would yield more-similar values in both.

text.text: Given that the optimal strategy for calculating both units and spans can differ within and across different languages, the selection of metrics becomes even more challenging for speech samples containing more than one language.
In our review of the existing literature, we observed five different approaches to the unit of speech and four different approaches to the span of speech (see Figure 1).

text.text: Each of these approaches will result in wildly different counts for datasets that contain more than one language, especially if those languages are typologically different like the ones we present in this paper.

text.text: The high diversity in implementation of MLU across different studies is likely to be driven in part by resource constraints in different research settings.
MLU is usually computed from written transcripts of speech behaviour.
However, transcription is a labour-intensive task, where one minute of speech may take up to an hour to transcribe, depending on the level of detail in the transcription protocol.

For example, in one recent study (see Woon et al., 2021), an in-house transcription protocol was developed (Loh et al., 2022) for transcription of multi-speaker, multilingual speech, with custom markup for linguistic features of interest.
text.formatted: For example, in one recent study (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">Woon et al., 2021)</ref>, an in-house transcription protocol was developed <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Loh et al., 2022)</ref> for transcription of multi-speaker, multilingual speech, with custom markup for linguistic features of interest.

text.text: It was estimated that transcriptions of parent-child speech took approximately 30 to 45 minutes of transcription per minute of speech, plus an additional 15 to 30 minutes of expert checking.

Initial training for new transcribers took 16 hours per transcriber (including practice and error correction), meaning that the true cost of transcription could easily reach one hour per minute of high engagement narrative speech (see Choo et al., forthcoming for more details about labour costs across languages).
text.formatted: Initial training for new transcribers took 16 hours per transcriber (including practice and error correction), meaning that the true cost of transcription could easily reach one hour per minute of high engagement narrative speech (see <ref type="bibr">Choo et al., forthcoming</ref> for more details about labour costs across languages).

text.text: As a way to reduce labour costs needed for transcriptions, researchers may look to using commercial transcribers or AI-based transcription tools.
However, those methods may not be ideal for transcribing recordings collected for research or clinical use.

First, while commercial transcribers working on monolingual speech (without specialist annotations) were often able to transcribe at a faster rate than in-house trained research staff, the transcriptions often differ from the norms of linguistically informed transcription protocols and are better suited for captioning professional speech or media content.

For example, commercial transcription services routinely omitted certain speech signals from the transcriptions, including speech errors, repairs, inaudible speech, and fillers such as 'aah' and 'mm'.

Since some of these features may be important for detailed linguistic analysis of utterance complexity, these transcriptions may not be well suited to recordings collected to study child language use or child-directed language use.

Second, for readily available AI-based transcription tools, there is a risk of privacy breaches since any recordings shared with the companies providing such services may be used to train their AI tools (Bäckström, 2025; Su, 2019).

text.text: Furthermore, in a clinical setting, practitioners may have limited time allocated to each patient, so time for data transcription may be scarce.
As a result, many researchers and practitioners in speech and language therapy have historically been interested in metrics of complexity that can be applied to small samples of speech.
Given the resource-intensive nature of in-house transcription, few researchers are able to compute metrics across large samples of recorded speech.

In our overview of the literature, only four papers reported conducting analysis on their entire recorded sample, while more than twenty papers subsampled from the original recording in a variety of ways.

For example, some researchers sampled a reduced number of utterances from each participant, ranging from 3 to 100 utterances (e.g., Casby, 2011; Gavin & Giles, 1996) or from 1 to 35 minutes of speech (Goh et al., 2008; Heilmann et al., 2010).

Overall, each of these subsampling approaches reduced the amount of speech processed for an individual recording.

Measurement diversity and the challenge of analytic flexibility.
In the sections above we reviewed the diversity of approaches to measurement of MLU-type metrics as an index of grammatical complexity in a speech sample.
Some of the diversity of measures arise from different ways of generating a sample, while others arise from different ways of computing metrics from an existing sample.
We have observed several decision points at which deriving a metric of MLU has substantial flexibility even after the primary data have been collected.
Taken together, a researcher has potentially 7 * 3 * 5 * 4 * 18 * 9 ways to produce a continuous MLU-like metric for a particular research target.
From a statistical perspective, this represents extremely high researcher degrees of freedom, also known as a large 'garden of forking paths' (Gelman & Loken, 2013).
text.formatted: From a statistical perspective, this represents extremely high researcher degrees of freedom, also known as a large 'garden of forking paths' <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Gelman & Loken, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The lack of clear decision pathways for adopting a particular measure of MLU means that there is substantial analytic flexibility in the field.
As summarised by Chambers (2017), where analytic flexibility is high, researchers run the risk of selecting a measure after testing which of multiple strategies produces the desired outcomes.
text.formatted: As summarised by <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chambers (2017)</ref>, where analytic flexibility is high, researchers run the risk of selecting a measure after testing which of multiple strategies produces the desired outcomes.

text.text: Moreover, in the existing literature, it is not always clear which analyses were based on a priori selection of measures, and which were based on post-hoc decision making after the results are known (see also Gelman & Loken, 2013; Simmons et al., 2011; Šoškić et al., 2022).

text.text: While it is not incorrect to investigate measures from different perspectives, best practices are those where the researcher clarifies which of their research process are exploratory (i.e., discussing among various options what patterns might exist in the data) versus hypothesis testing (i.e., evidence is used to test whether a theory predicts a particular outcome).

As mentioned, one of the goals of the current paper is to compare the measurement characteristics of different implementations of MLU on a large sample of speech using different measurements and subsampling approaches, and to use the results to propose a decision framework for preregister their metrics prior to hypothesis testing.

Given the variability in the existing literature, in the current paper, we report exploratory analyses designed to compare different implementations of MLU, and to see which measures reliably capture a developmental trajectory -that is to say, metrics that are positively correlated with the age of the child.
The end-goal is to present a decision tree that researchers and practitioners can use to decide which measurement of MLU-like syntactic complexity is best for their specific data and purposes.

This exploratory investigation serves as a baseline study of measurement properties, so that a single measure of MLU can be selected for a preregistered hypothesis test of an intervention that was conducted between time points.

text.text: In this study, we examined two speech units of interest.
First, we selected the morpheme rather than the word due to the high typological diversity of the main languages in our multilingual dataset.
We define a morpheme as the smallest unit of speech that conveys a meaning that could be parseable for a child using regular, productive morphological processes.
For example, 'quickly' is considered two morphemes, while 'mice' and 'backward' are both considered monomorphemic.

Second, we examined the utterance rather than the sentence, as parents did not typically speak in complete sentences to their children, and incomplete sentences can still convey meaningful information.

We used the definition of 'utterance' as documented in the BELA transcription protocol (see below; Loh et al., 2022; Sundaray, 2020), and consider complete sentences (that is, sentences that are marked by intonation and pauses between sentences) or, in lieu of complete sentences, "chunks that go together in intonation patterns" as utterances.

text.text: However, there are two limitations to using totals.
First, they are dependent on the length of the sample, which may be constrained by factors such as time available for recording, or child attention.
Second, a straightforward measure cannot differentiate between 100 one-word utterances and 10 ten-word utterances, meaning that there is no way to account for complexity of individual utterances.
For this reason, we also include metrics summarising the complexity of utterances (i.e., MLU-like metrics).
We calculated the Mean Length Utterance (MLU) in each transcript.
As the arithmetic mean is most appropriate for normal distributions, the MLU estimate may be influenced by outliers in the high tails of the utterance length distribution.
Hence, to accommodate deviations from normality, Median Length Utterance (Med-LU) was computed.
The Modal Length Utterance (Mod-LU) was also computed to examine the most frequently occurring length of utterance.

As deviations from normality were expected in the current sample, we included metrics that captured the lower bound of complexity, computed as the percentage of utterances consisting of a single morpheme.

In line with existing literature, we expect that parents of older children will use more complicated utterances in the book-sharing task, as compared to parents of younger children.

In the current exploration of metrics for MLU, we investigate distributional properties of the measures across the diverse sample, and use a cross-sectional design to investigate which metrics show the largest effect sizes in correlations between child age and complexity.
The study is therefore a multiverse-style model-refinement study designed to identify the best metric for a known relationship, and should not be considered as a standard hypothesis test.

Given the distributions observed here, previously reported relationships between MLU and age may be skewed by the upper tails of the data, rather than cleanly representing what is typical for the middle of the distribution for an individual speaker.
A more parsimonious approach would be to specify whether the target of interest is 'typical behaviour' or 'infrequent advanced behaviour'.

If the research target is typical behaviour, then a measure of central tendency should be selected on the basis of data distribution (mean only if normally distributed, otherwise, median); if the research target is 'infrequent advanced behaviour', an upper bound estimate such as those in the next section should be selected.

text.text: Hence, parental speech during wordless picture-book sharing contained significantly more speech and longer utterances when speaking to older children than to younger children.

Both the typical length of an utterance (MLU, Med-LU) and the length of the most extreme long utterances are shown to be longer for parents speaking to older children, with the latter increasing at a much faster rate than the typical length of an utterance.

As short utterances are characteristic of child-directed speech (e.g., Lester et al., 2022), by investigating the lower bounds of the distribution, we also observed that the proportion of very short utterances is smaller for parents speaking to older children.

text.text: The lower bound measure including all utterance types showed equivalent effect size to MLU and 1L metrics, making it as effective for capturing age-related complexity in parental speech as more traditional measures.
Med-LU is somewhat more powerful than MLU, and the upper bounds of complexity have an even larger effect size when more long utterances are included in the metric (i.e., 10L).
In addition to assessing measures of complexity across the whole sample, we further simulated how these measures compare on smaller subsamples of the corpus of speech.

As such, we created subsamples from the beginning of the recorded transcriptions to allow comparison between the full sample (all utterances) and a set of reduced samples (first 100, 90, 80, 70, 60, 50 and 10 utterances).

This simulation will allow us to evaluate the outcomes of different sampling approaches and propose a decision pathway for selecting the most appropriate measures for researchers and practitioners to use, according to the metrics of interest, the population of interest and the resources constraints that exist.

While total speech is relatively stable across sample sizes, it should be noted that this measure is heavily influenced by the nature of the speech elicitation task.

In our study, we elicited parental speech using a wordless picture book-sharing task, but the stability of this method may not apply in other speech contexts such as solving a structured puzzle using a fixed set of objects (see more in Discussion).

In panel 5B when we consider the measures of central tendency, the same general pattern is evident with larger samples resulting in larger effect sizes, with the exception of the smallest sample size (10 utterances) which is volatile to sample characteristics at that size.
Of these three measures, the mean and the median are reliably higher than the mode, suggesting that Mod-LU is the least useful measure of central tendency.
In panel 5C when we consider the lower bounds of complexity, even the smallest sample sizes provide effect sizes comparable to traditional MLU.
Most of the subsampling approaches fail to produce significant effects when interjections are excluded from utterance counts.
This highlights the important role interjections play in parental speech to younger children, as reductions in their use is a reliable property of conversational structure over development.
There is a stable advantage for measurements conducted over the whole corpus and a subset of the first 100 utterances as compared to smaller subsets.
In our initial simulation, we further compared subsets of 10 and 50 utterances (following extant literature) but found that none of the effect sizes were significant for 50 utterances.

Notably, measures conducted over only the first 10 utterances show a much less stable profile, with sudden discontinuities suggesting that extremely small samples may not provide good estimates of the overall complexity in the sample.
Furthermore, although 100 utterances may be ideal, not all parents will speak for 100 utterances, depending on the children's age.
Thus, we simulated the sets of utterances between 50 and 100 to identify the minimum number of utterances required to get a more robust measure of upper bound complexity.
Results show that none of the effect sizes were significant for 60, 70 and 80 utterances (although it was close to significance for 80).
When the subset included the first 90 utterances, the effect was significant from 6L onwards, suggesting this would be the minimum viable sample for an upper bound analysis.
We incorporate this threshold into our decision tree below.
We set out to investigate the relationship between a child's age and the MLU of parental childdirected speech in Singapore.

As most of the previous research on this topic has been conducted in communities of monolingual English speakers, this investigation has a specific focus on measurement of MLU as applied to a multilingual context with frequent translanguaging.

In terms of total speech, as expected, we observed a significant positive correlation for child age and quantity of speech, as measured by both total number of utterances and total number of morphemes.
In terms of central tendency for complexity, we found a significant positive correlation between child age and MLU-like metrics, as measured by both mean and median length of utterance.
In terms of the extreme upper bounds of complexity, child age correlated with various measures.

In particular, the mean length of the longest 10 utterances (10L) provided a more stable measure of upper bound extremes than the mean length when calculated over fewer utterances (e.g., the single longest utterance, 1L).

For the extreme lower bounds of complexity, we also observed that the percentage of monomorphemic child-directed utterances was inversely correlated with age, and this effect was strongest when all utterance types (including interjections) were included in the data sample.

When conducted across the whole dataset, MLU, Med-LU, percent monomorphemic utterances and longest single utterance all correlated with age, at equivalent effect sizes (ρ = .20), suggesting that multiple metrics are valid for a general overview of 'complexity' development, and that the unique characteristics of a particular dataset and research constraints may be used to guide decisions about which metric to select.

The only metrics that routinely exceed this effect size are the total morpheme count (how much a parent talks to their child over the course of the book-sharing) and the 10L metric (the average length of the ten longest utterances of a parent to their child).

Overall, in multilingual Singapore, where over 99% of the parents in our study used more than one language with their child during a naturalistic book-sharing session, we see that parental speech grew increasingly complex as children grew older.

We argue that language-inclusive metrics (including speech in all languages, and all kinds of speech) provide the best estimates of speech complexity in communities where translanguaging is prevalent.

text.text: Challenge: Grammatical complexity such as MLU can be measured in myriad ways in a parent/child speech sample, potentially leading to high researcher degrees of freedom (Chambers, 2017)).
text.formatted: Challenge: Grammatical complexity such as MLU can be measured in myriad ways in a parent/child speech sample, potentially leading to high researcher degrees of freedom <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Chambers, 2017)</ref>).

text.text: In the current paper, we conducted a large-scale exploratory analysis of multiple metrics, with a goal to characterise different measurement properties.
To reduce researcher degrees of freedom, best practice is to specify which metrics will be analysed prior to data collection/viewing.

An evidence-based decision-pathway may help researchers to select metrics depending on study characteristics and resource context, prior to observing data, as would be suitable for a preregistered protocol.
Action Points: Use of a metric-selection decision pathway allows preregistration of metrics when characteristics of a sample have not yet been observed.

Challenge: 'Word' as a unit of analysis comes from a history of English language research which aligns poorly with other linguistic contexts, including languages with different writing systems, typologically diverse languages, and multilingual samples.

As our sample includes data from four languages (English, Mandarin, Malay and Tamil), we elected to run all analyses reported here using morphemes as the basic unit of measurement, and to include data from all languages that make up the linguistic repertoire of the speaker.
This approach prioritises inclusivity over linguistic purity, and may be suitable in a variety of multilingual/diglossic contexts.
For further discussion about the decision to use morphemes, see Choo et al. (forthcoming).
text.formatted: For further discussion about the decision to use morphemes, see <ref type="bibr">Choo et al. (forthcoming)</ref>.

text.text: Action points: Future work should consider language characteristics of the sample before determining the unit of comparison (words versus morphemes).

Morphemes may be the most equitable unit of measurement for grammatical complexity, whether they occur in monomorphemic words in isolating languages, or in multimorphemic words in agglutinating languages.

Span of speech in the measure Challenge: 'Sentence' as a unit of analysis comes from a history of English language research which aligns poorly with other linguistic contexts, such as languages with topic-comment grammar, and multilingual, translanguaged samples.
Linguistic definitions of what constitutes a well-formed 'sentence' (cf., Brown, 1973) do not align with the ways that caregivers structure their speech for children in all contexts.
text.formatted: Linguistic definitions of what constitutes a well-formed 'sentence' (cf., <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brown, 1973)</ref> do not align with the ways that caregivers structure their speech for children in all contexts.

text.text: As some languages are better characterised by topic-comment grammatical structure, selection of utterance over sentence may be most flexible and inclusive.
We selected utterance as the span of speech rather than sentence to flexibly account for both linguistic structure and pragmatic factors in parent-child speech.
Action points: Decisions about the span of speech over which complexity is measured should take into account different linguistic structures and the pragmatic realities of parent-child speech.
The span of a measure should be guided by the age of the child and the language context.
Further research may be needed to validate metrics used for data with a different underlying structure, or with children of different age ranges.
Challenge: Speech recorded in naturalistic parent-child interactions are highly variable, and different elicitation and sub-sampling techniques will highlight different speech features.

Differences in duration or total amount of speech may form part of the developmental trajectory for parent/child speech, meaning that a short time-bound subsample may 'flatten' developmental differences.
The metrics reported here come from speech samples which ranged in duration from 2 to 35 minutes with a median duration of 7'15 minutes.

In general, the book-sharing sessions were longer for older children (in terms of raw duration, as well as total count of morphemes), and more complex (as demonstrated in the different MLU-like metrics reported).

In the current study, we did not set a threshold for the minimum duration or number of utterances for inclusion in the sample for analysis, as we had no a priori reason for determining what constituted insufficient speech.

In wordless picture-book sharing recordings in our dataset, many measures of complexity did not show significant developmental trajectories in the shortest subsamples, although the proportion of monomorphemic utterances (including interjections) remained reliable even for very small samples.

The minimum amount of speech recorded or processed for an evaluation of grammatical complexity should be guided by the age of the child, the kind of speech under investigation (e.g., naturalistic storytelling; picture description; task oriented discussion; narrative recall; etc), and the purpose of the evaluation (e.g., norming typical behaviour; inclusion in a developmental battery as a dependent variable in a study; assessment of a child's language skills in a clinical context).
Further research may be needed to validate metrics used for data with a different underlying structure to those reported in the current report.

For example, speech recorded for clinical evaluation of a child's language skills may be structured differently, and further research with controlled speech samples may be needed to validate the metrics reported here.
Challenge: Underlying data distribution is rarely reported when using common measures of central tendency such as MLU.
Means are often used as a default summary measure, however the mean is a poor measure of central tendency unless the underlying sample is normally distributed.
In our sample, we clearly demonstrate non-normal distributions in parents' child-directed speech in our sample.
Non-normal distributions are also characteristic of children's utterances, which typically contain many extremely-short utterances and few extremely-long utterances (Brown, 1973).
text.formatted: Non-normal distributions are also characteristic of children's utterances, which typically contain many extremely-short utterances and few extremely-long utterances <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: As such, the median is a truer representation of central tendency in grammatical complexity.
Choice of mean in a nonnormally distributed sample essentially skews the measure towards the upper bound of utterance length.
Researchers may want to consider whether their research target is better construed as an estimate of upper bound complexity.

Note that in correlations with child age, the median length of parental utterance has a lower intercept (i.e., the median is a lower value as it is less skewed by high outliers), however the effect size for median is almost identical to the effect size computed for mean.

Action points: Future studies should check the data distribution of utterance lengths in their sample before deciding whether to select median or mean as a measure of typical linguistic complexity, and consider whether their use-case would benefit from a measure of extreme (upper bound) language use instead.

Upper bound metrics: Longest X utterances Challenge: The long tails of data distribution for utterance length mean that the longest utterances are unusual for the individual, however they may contain important evidence of development at its limits.

When sampling from the extreme upper bound of complexity, we found that sampling from a larger number of utterances provides a more stable estimate, with larger effect sizes for 10 longest utterances than for samples including fewer tokens.
Computing an upper bound of complexity over the 10 longest parental utterances provides an effect size boost from ρ = .2 to ρ = .3.
However, in resource constrained contexts, the 6 longest utterances from a sample of 90 utterances may be a practical minimum sample size.

It is notable that in our sample, the upper bound of complexity estimate provided the strongest effect size in correlations with age, suggesting it is a powerful measure of parental speech complexity for parent-child speech interactions with children across this age range (8-40 months).
Researchers and clinicians should use estimates of upper bound complexity instead of the measures of central tendency if their research aims to highlight the most advanced behaviours available.
Estimates of upper bounds of complexity benefit from including more utterances in the sample.
Detailed recommendations can be found in the decision tree (Figure 6).

text.text: Lower bound metrics: monomorph emic utterances Challenge: Although often overlooked, the shortest utterances in parentchild speech provide insights into the development of conversational complexity.
In the current study, we demonstrated that lower bound estimates of parental utterance length can be as effective in correlations with age as measures of central tendency (i.e., similar effect size).
We also observed the effect of age was stronger when interjections/languageless utterances were included in the metric.

This holds true even for the smallest subsample of the first 10 utterances, and for the second smallest subsample of the first 50 utterances -the proportion of monomorphemic utterances has the strongest effect size which is larger than the total or central tendency metric.
This lower bound estimate provides an effect size that is almost as strong as traditional counts of MLU, showing how prevalent interjections are in early child-directed speech.
Traditional interpretations tend to treat interjections merely as emotional reflexive outbursts or 'response cries' (cf. Goffman, 1978).
text.formatted: Traditional interpretations tend to treat interjections merely as emotional reflexive outbursts or 'response cries' (cf. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Goffman, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: However, work by conversation analysis researchers have shown how interjections like hm?
assist parents in repair-initiation at MLU Stage 1 (Corrin, 2010), and how interjections like mm hm, huh?

text.text: Following this logic, we argue that speech that might be classified as 'languageless' (Loh et al., 2022), or as 'interjections' (Brown, 1973) can meaningfully be included in lower bound metrics of parental speech, and enhances the effect size of lower bound metrics.

text.text: Action Points: When sampling from the extreme lower bound of complexity, all parental utterance types should be included, including interjections and utterances that may be considered 'languageless' or 'non-meaning-bearing' (e.g., fillers).
Further investigations will be needed to understand whether a similar pattern is observed in metrics of child speech complexity as well as parental child-directed speech.

Decisions on the metric of interest should be explained clearly in light of specific research targets, theoretical considerations, and/or methodological constraints. Brown's (1973) original conception of MLU provided an estimate of central tendency for a child's speech complexity, averaged across all utterances in a recording.

text.text: He also noted that "as the mean length of utterance gets longer so does the upper bound or longest utterance" (p. 184).

Our illustration of the distributional characteristics of utterance length across a parent-child conversation shows how the extreme upper tails of a distribution essentially skew the mean towards the upper bound.
A more parsimonious approach is to consider lower bound, upper bound and central tendency as discrete, measurable characteristics of speech behaviour.

Given that the current paper shows all three parts of the complexity distribution (lower bound, central tendency, upper bound) differ significantly across the developmental age range of the current study, researchers can select the metric that best aligns with their specific use-case (i.e., which metric best aligns with their research interests or clinical use) and methodological constraints (i.e., labour available for processing), or report all three metrics for completeness.
Action Points: Future research will benefit from theoretical and methodological justifications for the selection of metrics of speech complexity.
Selection of metrics should be clearly stated (with justifications) at the point of preregistration.

text.text: Decisions about whether the whole sample of speech or a subsample of speech are included in analysis should be clearly explained with attention to resource constraints such as time available, cost of transcription/annotation, and technical resources available for automated pre-processing.
According to our measures of change over development, sampling from the whole distribution provides the most reliable metrics of complexity.

To simulate different recording durations or resource-limits on transcriptions, we compared correlations of age of child with the different measures of complexity calculated over different sample durations, starting from the first utterance (first 10, first 50 to first 100 in intervals of 10, all utterances).
When subsampling, there is increasing stabilisation of effect size with increasing sample size.
Given this finding, in resourceconstrained contexts, particular approaches to subsampling should have or theoretical or methodological justifications.
Action points: Researchers aiming to use measures of complexity as key metrics in their research should plan for adequate resources for full transcription of the entire sample where possible.
However, where resource constraints exist, researchers should clearly state their data subsampling approach (with justifications).
An example decision tree is provided in Figure 6, as would be appropriate for inclusion in a preregistration or protocol registration.

text.text: Decisions about handling multilingual data can influence the characterisation of individuals and communities, and should be clearly justified.

As translanguaging is normal linguistic behaviour in many intergenerational bilingual communities, translanguaged and nonmajority language content should be included in MLU-like metrics if possible, and its removal requires strong justification.

We have shown elsewhere that within-utterance translanguaging was observed for 80% of parents in the Talk Together Study sample, at a median translanguaging rate of 5% (Styles et al., 2022a), making it a normal part of daily linguistic interaction between parents and children in the local context.
text.formatted: We have shown elsewhere that within-utterance translanguaging was observed for 80% of parents in the Talk Together Study sample, at a median translanguaging rate of 5% <ref type="bibr">(Styles et al., 2022a)</ref>, making it a normal part of daily linguistic interaction between parents and children in the local context.

text.text: To form an accurate representation of everyday speech, translanguaged utterances were included in the metrics reported in this paper, and a holistic MLU is reported (not separated into different languages).
To include all languages in the metric, it was necessary to use morphemes as the unit of analysis.
In some research contexts, conducting transcription and morpheme-counts may be more resource intensive for some linguistic content than for others.
The labour cost of this approach is high, as we outline elsewhere (Choo et al., forthcoming).
text.formatted: The labour cost of this approach is high, as we outline elsewhere <ref type="bibr">(Choo et al., forthcoming)</ref>.

text.text: Semi-automated processes such as use of automated morphemisers can mitigate these costs in some languages, although their use is limited by current biases in the datasets on which they have been trained (Styles et al., 2023.
text.formatted: Semi-automated processes such as use of automated morphemisers can mitigate these costs in some languages, although their use is limited by current biases in the datasets on which they have been trained <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Styles et al., 2023</ref>.

text.text: Researchers working in monolingual majority contexts should think carefully about whether it is possible to include non-majority linguistic content in their metrics, as selective exclusion of some linguistic content may introduce structured biases in their metrics.

Researchers working in multilingual communities should plan for multilingual metrics where possible, and plan to use morphemes as the unit of analysis to allow better cross-language coherence among typologically distinct languages.

Based on the above operationalisations, we present a decision tree (Figure 6) as a reproducible, preregisterable pathway for deciding which measurement of MLU-like syntactic complexity to use in a given context.
text.formatted: Based on the above operationalisations, we present a decision tree (Figure <ref type="figure">6</ref>) as a reproducible, preregisterable pathway for deciding which measurement of MLU-like syntactic complexity to use in a given context.

text.text: The decision tree allows a researcher to state which of their research features are known (e.g., is the target of the research 'typical speech' or 'unusual extremes'), and which are unknown (e.g., normal vs. non-normal distribution), and subsequently follow the decision tree after data are collected, to finalize the metric for inclusion in analysis.
The decision tree provides two tangible benefits.

First, in the case of an unexpected outcome (e.g., less labour available for transcribing/morpheme segmentation of speech), the tree provides a reasoned pathway for selection of the next-most-suitable approach.
Second, consulting the decision tree may allow a researcher to refine their procedure during research planning to ensure more robust metrics.

Decision tree for selecting best MLU-like measure From the flowchart, researchers and practitioners can decide on the metric of study according to their availability of transcriptions (full transcripts, partial transcripts), research/clinical interests (lower bound of complexity, central tendency, upper bound of complexity) and amount of data in their sample (number of utterances, length of recording, random sample).
We illustrate the use of the decision tree with two example scenarios.
(Schematics are presented in Figures 7 and 8; see Supplementary Figures 2 and 3 for full versions with text.)
text.formatted: (Schematics are presented in Figures <ref type="figure">7</ref> and <ref type="figure">8</ref>; see Supplementary Figures <ref type="figure">2</ref> and <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref> for full versions with text.)

text.text: Scenario 1) a research team has access to a large corpus of child-directed speech across a wide age range of children that has already been fully transcribed.

In line with existing literature, the team expects that older children will be exposed to speech of higher complexity speech than when compared to younger children, and they would like to preregister an analysis plan including a measure of speech complexity, such as MLU.
Since both central tendency and upper bound complexity have been shown to correlate strongly with age, the research team might consider including both estimates in their study design.

Recommendations: For a measure of central tendency, both mean and median have been shown to correlate strongly with to child age, but the choice should be determined by the distribution of the underlying data.
In particular, for non-normally distributed data, we recommend selecting the median utterance length as the measure of central tendency.

Prior to inspecting data from the study, the research team may not be able to estimate data distribution, but they may register the pathway, as it has clear guidance on which should be used once data is seen.

For measures of upper bound complexity, the more stable relationships between complexity and age were observed when a larger number of upper bound utterances were included in the metric, meaning that a metric computed over the 10 longest utterances (10L) is indicated.

Hence, following the decision points in the flowchart, the research team could elect to focus on central tendency (MLU or Med-LU depending on distribution), upper bound complexity (MLU of the 10 longest utterances in a sample of at least 100 utterances), or both, in a preregistered design with precise operationalization of metrics prior to observing the data.
Decision tree simulation for a researcher with access to full transcriptions of long samples of speech, and/or resources to produce them.
Scenario 2) A clinician has a few minutes to gather a sample of parent-child speech in a context with high resource constraints.
In the limited time available, the clinician expects the parent to produce about 50 utterances.

In line with existing literature, they expect complexity of speech to increase with child age, meaning that a dyad with unexpectedly low speech complexity may be flagged for further investigation for speech, language, or communication difficulties.
Their initial interest may be in evaluating the upper bound of speech complexity, representing the most complex speech the child might be routinely exposed to.

Recommendations: Metrics of upper bound complexity were shown to be unstable for samples of speech with fewer than 90 utterances, meaning that measures of upper bound complexity should be used with caution in a small sample, or an alternative metric used.
Since measures of central tendency require transcription of large samples to be effective, they may not be suitable in a resource constrained environment.

If the language sample can be increased to include at least 90 utterances, the mean of the 6 longest utterances (6L) would be a suitable metric, although the mean of the 10 longest utterances (10L) in a sample of 100 would be even better.
If the language sample cannot be increased, then a measure of lower bound complexity would be more stable, such as the proportion of monomorphemic utterances including interjections.

In this way, access to a decision aid during planning allows researchers and clinicians to decide whether to devote resources to collecting more data at the point of evaluation, transcribing/coding more speech after the evaluation, or to use an alternative metric which requires less offline coding.
Decision tree simulation for someone who is more resource-pressed
The aim of this paper was three-fold.

First, we provided an overview of how MLU is counted and analysed in literature then explored measurement characteristics of MLU-like metrics in a large corpus of child-directed speech from parents in multilingual Singapore.
We compared different methods of computing MLU and showed the challenges of trying to fit a multilingual translanguaging-heavy dataset into commonly used MLU metrics.

Next, using our dataset as an example, we showed that these MLU-like metrics are better suited as measures of grammatical complexity and gathered our suggestions for researchers and clinicians who are looking for new ways to examine grammatical complexity and/or also work in bi/multilingual communities.

Third, we also simulated conditions where researchers or clinicians may be short on time or labour, and would require a metric that is quicker to administer while still providing viable metrics (see Choo et al., forthcoming for detailed discussion of labour costs).
text.formatted: Third, we also simulated conditions where researchers or clinicians may be short on time or labour, and would require a metric that is quicker to administer while still providing viable metrics (see <ref type="bibr">Choo et al.,</ref> forthcoming for detailed discussion of labour costs).

text.text: From our dataset, we observed a general trend for increasing complexity with increasing age of the child, though some metrics showed stronger correlations than others.

In our comparison of metrics, we demonstrate that all three parts of the utterance length distribution (lower bound, central tendency, upper bound) are informative for characterising complexity in the speech of parents talking with children of different ages.

Although the current dataset focusses on parental speech to typically developing children across a wide age range (8 to 40 months), it is possible that the different measures reported here may have advantages when working with different kinds of data.

For example, when working on speech samples from very young children, second language learners, or speakers with language delays and disorders, lower bound estimates may prove to be more informative than measures that rely on longer utterances.

By contrast, where the research target is aligned with low frequency utterances of unusually high complexity, upper bound estimates may be more informative for contexts focusing on individual differences.

Future research will be needed to investigate how the variety of metrics can best be applied to a variety of research contexts, however, by including less-well-known MLU-like metrics in the review of measures, we have shown that non-traditional measures may be valuable to practitioners working in under-resourced contexts, without compromising the validity of the metrics.
To aid in decision making, we present a decision tree as a reproducible, pre-registerable pathway for deciding which measurement of MLU-like syntactic complexity is best for data of different types.

The current paper demonstrates the use of these metrics in a multilingual context where translanguaging is prevalent with a focus on the morpheme as the key unit of analysis (see Choo et al., forthcoming for detailed discussion of how morphemes are better suited for multilingual contexts).

text.text: While further research will be needed to unpack the nuanced relationship between morphology and complexity in different languages, this paper is a proof-of-concept for approaches that focus on inclusion of all linguistic content in messy, real-world contexts over traditional approaches to classifying and separating speech into discrete named-language categories.
